claim: Within 2–4 weeks of SARS-CoV-2 infection, most individuals generate detectable levels of several antibody subtypes (immunoglobulin A, M, G) directed against different domains of the virus (Nucleocapsid protein, Spike protein, receptor-binding domain of Spike).
source: Within 2–4 weeks of infection, most individuals generate detectable levels of several antibody subtypes (immunoglobulin A, M, G) directed against different domains of the virus (Nucleocapsid protein, Spike protein, receptor-binding domain of Spike), which gradually decline over time (Seow et al., 2020; Brochot et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2021a; Long et al., 2020; Gaebler et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research (Seow et al., 2020; Brochot et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2021a; Long et al., 2020; Gaebler et al., 2021).

claim: Antibody levels generated following SARS-CoV-2 infection gradually decline over time.
source: Within 2–4 weeks of infection, most individuals generate detectable levels of several antibody subtypes (immunoglobulin A, M, G) directed against different domains of the virus (Nucleocapsid protein, Spike protein, receptor-binding domain of Spike), which gradually decline over time (Seow et al., 2020; Brochot et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2021a; Long et al., 2020; Gaebler et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research (Seow et al., 2020; Brochot et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2021a; Long et al., 2020; Gaebler et al., 2021).

claim: Anti-Nucleocapsid antibodies are generated following SARS-CoV-2 infection but not by any current SARS-CoV-2 vaccines.
source: Anti-Nucleocapsid antibodies are generated following infection but not by any current SARS-CoV-2 vaccines, while anti-Spike antibodies are generated following infection or vaccination.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of vaccine design and antibody responses.

claim: Anti-Spike antibodies are generated following SARS-CoV-2 infection or vaccination.
source: Anti-Nucleocapsid antibodies are generated following infection but not by any current SARS-CoV-2 vaccines, while anti-Spike antibodies are generated following infection or vaccination.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of vaccine design and antibody responses.

claim: Levels of anti-Spike antibodies correlate with SARS-CoV-2-neutralising anti-receptor-binding domain antibody titre.
source: Levels of anti-Spike antibodies correlate with SARS-CoV-2-neutralising anti-receptor-binding domain antibody titre (Perkmann et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research (Perkmann et al., 2021).

claim: A similar profile of antibody induction with subsequent waning is observed after vaccination against SARS-CoV-2.
source: A similar profile of antibody induction with subsequent waning is observed after vaccination against SARS-CoV-2 (Shrotri et al., 2021a; Shrotri et al., 2021b; Matsunaga et al., 2022; Pegu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research (Shrotri et al., 2021a; Shrotri et al., 2021b; Matsunaga et al., 2022; Pegu et al., 2021).

claim: Waning of antibody levels are likely correlated with observed reductions in vaccine effectiveness over time.
source: Waning of antibody levels are likely correlated with observed reductions in vaccine effectiveness over time (Pouwels et al., 2021; UKHSA, 2021; Lopez Bernal et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research (Pouwels et al., 2021; UKHSA, 2021; Lopez Bernal et al., 2021).

claim: Reduced antibody neutralising activity and vaccine effectiveness have been observed for variants of concern in comparison to ancestral SARS-CoV-2.
source: Reduced antibody neutralising activity and vaccine effectiveness have been observed for variants of concern in comparison to ancestral SARS-CoV-2 (UKHSA, 2021; Collie et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2022; Nemet et al., 2022; Cheng et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research (UKHSA, 2021; Collie et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2022; Nemet et al., 2022; Cheng et al., 2022).

claim: Anti-Spike antibody levels have been found to be inversely proportional to risk of future infection.
source: Anti-Spike antibody levels have been found to be inversely proportional to risk of future infection, and so identified as a correlate of protection (Goldblatt et al., 2022a; Perry et al., 2022; Gilbert et al., 2022; Goldblatt et al., 2022b; Feng et al., 2021; Dimeglio et al., 2022a; Dimeglio et al., 2022b; Khoury et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research (Goldblatt et al., 2022a; Perry et al., 2022; Gilbert et al., 2022; Goldblatt et al., 2022b; Feng et al., 2021; Dimeglio et al., 2022a; Dimeglio et al., 2022b; Khoury et al., 2021).

claim: Anti-Spike antibody levels are identified as a correlate of protection against SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Anti-Spike antibody levels have been found to be inversely proportional to risk of future infection, and so identified as a correlate of protection (Goldblatt et al., 2022a; Perry et al., 2022; Gilbert et al., 2022; Goldblatt et al., 2022b; Feng et al., 2021; Dimeglio et al., 2022a; Dimeglio et al., 2022b; Khoury et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research (Goldblatt et al., 2022a; Perry et al., 2022; Gilbert et al., 2022; Goldblatt et al., 2022b; Feng et al., 2021; Dimeglio et al., 2022a; Dimeglio et al., 2022b; Khoury et al., 2021).

claim: Goldblatt et al. estimated protective thresholds of 154 (95% CI: 42, 559) BAU/mL for wild-type SARS-CoV-2.
source: Goldblatt et al. estimated protective thresholds of 154 (95% CI: 42, 559) and 171 (95% CI: 57, 519) BAU/mL for wild-type and alpha variant SARS-CoV-2 respectively and an initial estimate range of 36–490 BAU/ml for delta variant (Goldblatt et al., 2022b), while Feng et al., 2021 estimated 80% vaccine effectiveness against alpha variant for levels above 264 (95% CI: 108, 806) BAU/mL.
evidence: Supported by citation to published research (Goldblatt et al., 2022b).

claim: Goldblatt et al. estimated protective thresholds of 171 (95% CI: 57, 519) BAU/mL for alpha variant SARS-CoV-2.
source: Goldblatt et al. estimated protective thresholds of 154 (95% CI: 42, 559) and 171 (95% CI: 57, 519) BAU/mL for wild-type and alpha variant SARS-CoV-2 respectively and an initial estimate range of 36–490 BAU/ml for delta variant (Goldblatt et al., 2022b), while Feng et al., 2021 estimated 80% vaccine effectiveness against alpha variant for levels above 264 (95% CI: 108, 806) BAU/mL.
evidence: Supported by citation to published research (Goldblatt et al., 2022b).

claim: Goldblatt et al. estimated an initial estimate range of 36–490 BAU/ml for delta variant SARS-CoV-2.
source: Goldblatt et al. estimated protective thresholds of 154 (95% CI: 42, 559) and 171 (95% CI: 57, 519) BAU/mL for wild-type and alpha variant SARS-CoV-2 respectively and an initial estimate range of 36–490 BAU/ml for delta variant (Goldblatt et al., 2022b), while Feng et al., 2021 estimated 80% vaccine effectiveness against alpha variant for levels above 264 (95% CI: 108, 806) BAU/mL.
evidence: Supported by citation to published research (Goldblatt et al., 2022b).

claim: Feng et al., 2021 estimated 80% vaccine effectiveness against alpha variant for levels above 264 (95% CI: 108, 806) BAU/mL.
source: Goldblatt et al. estimated protective thresholds of 154 (95% CI: 42, 559) and 171 (95% CI: 57, 519) BAU/mL for wild-type and alpha variant SARS-CoV-2 respectively and an initial estimate range of 36–490 BAU/ml for delta variant (Goldblatt et al., 2022b), while Feng et al., 2021 estimated 80% vaccine effectiveness against alpha variant for levels above 264 (95% CI: 108, 806) BAU/mL.
evidence: Supported by citation to published research (Feng et al., 2021).

claim: Dimeglio et al. estimated that levels of more than 6000 BAU/mL were needed for protection against omicron variant BA.1.
source: Dimeglio et al. estimated much higher levels of more than 6000 BAU/mL were needed for protection against omicron variant BA.1, while no relationship was found between infection and antibody level for BA.2 (Dimeglio et al., 2022b).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research (Dimeglio et al., 2022b).

claim: No relationship was found between infection and antibody level for omicron variant BA.2.
source: Dimeglio et al. estimated much higher levels of more than 6000 BAU/mL were needed for protection against omicron variant BA.1, while no relationship was found between infection and antibody level for BA.2 (Dimeglio et al., 2022b).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research (Dimeglio et al., 2022b).

claim: Lower antibody levels following both first and second vaccinations have been observed in individuals with particular comorbidities (including cancer, renal disease, and hepatic disease).
source: Lower antibody levels following both first and second vaccinations have been observed in individuals with particular comorbidities (including cancer, renal disease, and hepatic disease; Parry et al., 2021; Monin et al., 2021; Kearns et al., 2021), individuals using immunosuppressant medications (Shrotri et al., 2021a; Shrotri et al., 2021b; Parry et al., 2021; Monin et al., 2021), and individuals identified from electronic health records data as of moderate or high risk of COVID-19 complications (according to UK government prior 'Shielded Patient List' criteria of conditions, ongoing treatments, and medications) (Shrotri et al., 2021a; Shrotri et al., 2021b; GOV.UK, 2022b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research (Parry et al., 2021; Monin et al., 2021; Kearns et al., 2021).

claim: Lower antibody levels following both first and second vaccinations have been observed in individuals using immunosuppressant medications.
source: Lower antibody levels following both first and second vaccinations have been observed in individuals with particular comorbidities (including cancer, renal disease, and hepatic disease; Parry et al., 2021; Monin et al., 2021; Kearns et al., 2021), individuals using immunosuppressant medications (Shrotri et al., 2021a; Shrotri et al., 2021b; Parry et al., 2021; Monin et al., 2021), and individuals identified from electronic health records data as of moderate or high risk of COVID-19 complications (according to UK government prior 'Shielded Patient List' criteria of conditions, ongoing treatments, and medications) (Shrotri et al., 2021a; Shrotri et al., 2021b; GOV.UK, 2022b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research (Shrotri et al., 2021a; Shrotri et al., 2021b; Parry et al., 2021; Monin et al., 2021).

claim: Lower antibody levels following both first and second vaccinations have been observed in individuals identified from electronic health records data as of moderate or high risk of COVID-19 complications (according to UK government prior 'Shielded Patient List' criteria).
source: Lower antibody levels following both first and second vaccinations have been observed in individuals with particular comorbidities (including cancer, renal disease, and hepatic disease; Parry et al., 2021; Monin et al., 2021; Kearns et al., 2021), individuals using immunosuppressant medications (Shrotri et al., 2021a; Shrotri et al., 2021b; Parry et al., 2021; Monin et al., 2021), and individuals identified from electronic health records data as of moderate or high risk of COVID-19 complications (according to UK government prior 'Shielded Patient List' criteria of conditions, ongoing treatments, and medications) (Shrotri et al., 2021a; Shrotri et al., 2021b; GOV.UK, 2022b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research (Shrotri et al., 2021a; Shrotri et al., 2021b; GOV.UK, 2022b).

claim: Antibody levels were measured in 9361 individuals at two timepoints – 4256 individuals from TwinsUK and 4622 individuals from ALSPAC during April and May 2021.
source: Antibody levels were measured in 9361 individuals at two timepoints – 4256 individuals from TwinsUK and 4622 individuals from ALSPAC during April and May 2021 (referred to throughout as Q2 [calendar year quarter 2] testing), and 3575 individuals from TwinsUK in follow-up testing from November 2021 to January 2022 (referred to throughout as Q4 [quarter 4] testing).
evidence: Based on data collected in the study as described in the Methods section.

claim: 3575 individuals from TwinsUK were tested in follow-up testing from November 2021 to January 2022.
source: Antibody levels were measured in 9361 individuals at two timepoints – 4256 individuals from TwinsUK and 4622 individuals from ALSPAC during April and May 2021 (referred to throughout as Q2 [calendar year quarter 2] testing), and 3575 individuals from TwinsUK in follow-up testing from November 2021 to January 2022 (referred to throughout as Q4 [quarter 4] testing).
evidence: Based on data collected in the study as described in the Methods section.

claim: Response rates for antibody testing were: TwinsUK Q2: 87%, TwinsUK Q4: 80%, ALSPAC Q2: 79%.
source: Response rates, as the percentage who returned sample after consenting and being sent a sample collection kit, were as follows: TwinsUK Q2: 87%, TwinsUK Q4: 80%, ALSPAC Q2: 79%.
evidence: Based on data collected in the study as described in the Results section.

claim: Individuals who had received more vaccinations at either timepoint were older, more likely to be on the UK 'Shielded Patient List', and had lower self-rated health, compared with those with fewer vaccinations.
source: Consistent with the tiered UK vaccination campaign, individuals who had received more vaccinations at either timepoint were older, more likely to be on the UK 'Shielded Patient List' (GOV.UK, 2022b), and had lower self-rated health, compared with those with fewer vaccinations.
evidence: Based on data collected in the study as described in the Results section.

claim: Participants were predominantly female and the vast majority were of white ethnicity in both cohorts.
source: Participants were predominantly female and the vast majority were of white ethnicity in both cohorts, consistent with the broader composition of both cohorts.
evidence: Based on data collected in the study as described in the Results section.

claim: The median anti-Spike antibody levels in individuals who had received a third vaccination were over 10-fold higher than for individuals after second vaccination: 13700 BAU/mL after third vaccination, 1300 BAU/mL after second vaccination, 50 BAU/mL after first vaccination.
source: The median anti-Spike antibody levels in individuals who had received a third vaccination (unadjusted for time since vaccination) were over 10-fold higher than for individuals after second vaccination: 13700 BAU/mL after third vaccination, 1300 BAU/mL after second vaccination, 50 BAU/mL after first vaccination (Figure 1, detailed univariable splits of anti-Spike levels given in Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Based on data collected in the study and presented in Figure 1.

claim: 90% of individuals after third vaccination had antibody levels greater than 5000 BAU/mL.
source: There were also large increases in absolute levels for individuals at the bottom of the antibody level distribution after third vaccination, with 90% having level greater than 5000 BAU/mL, close to the estimated 6000 BAU/mL threshold estimated to confer partial protection against the omicron variant (Dimeglio et al., 2022b).
evidence: Based on data collected in the study as described in the Results section.

claim: The antibody level distribution after third vaccination was relatively narrower compared with earlier vaccination.
source: The antibody level distribution after third vaccination was relatively narrower compared with earlier vaccination (median:IQR ratios of 0.54, 0.27, and 0.89 among Q2 single-vaccinated, Q4 double-vaccinated, and Q4 triple-vaccinated sub-samples, respectively), with smaller scale-factor differences between those with median and lowest levels (median:10th percentile ratios of 5.6, 11.8, and 2.7 among Q2 single-vaccinated, Q4 double-vaccinated, and Q4 triple-vaccinated sub-samples, respectively).
evidence: Based on data collected in the study as described in the Results section.

claim: Within TwinsUK Q4 results, median antibody levels up to 16 weeks since third vaccination were highest in individuals sampled 2–3 weeks after vaccination (median: 24600 BAU/mL, n=203).
source: Within TwinsUK Q4 results, median antibody levels up to 16 weeks since third vaccination were highest in individuals sampled 2–3 weeks after vaccination (median: 24600 BAU/mL, n=203) (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on data collected in the study and presented in Figure 2.

claim: There was no evidence of decline in median antibody levels between 8 and 16 weeks after third vaccination (Mann-Kendall trend test in median levels at 8+ weeks, p=0.60).
source: Although median antibody levels decreased between 2 and 8 weeks after third vaccination, there was no evidence of further decline between 8 and 16 weeks (Mann-Kendall trend test in median levels at 8+ weeks, p=0.60), and high absolute levels of antibodies were sustained (8+ weeks median = 9200 BAU/mL [IQR: 5800–16000 BAU/mL], n=519).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of data collected in the study.

claim: High absolute levels of antibodies were sustained 8+ weeks after third vaccination (median = 9200 BAU/mL [IQR: 5800–16000 BAU/mL], n=519).
source: Although median antibody levels decreased between 2 and 8 weeks after third vaccination, there was no evidence of further decline between 8 and 16 weeks (Mann-Kendall trend test in median levels at 8+ weeks, p=0.60), and high absolute levels of antibodies were sustained (8+ weeks median = 9200 BAU/mL [IQR: 5800–16000 BAU/mL], n=519).
evidence: Based on data collected in the study as described in the Results section.

claim: Post-vaccination SARS CoV-2 infection (between first vaccination and Q4 testing) was recorded in 276 of 2993 (9.2%) individuals within TwinsUK.
source: Within TwinsUK, post-vaccination SARS CoV-2 infection (between first vaccination and Q4 testing) was recorded in 276 of 2993 (9.2%) individuals (further details related to post-vaccination infection given in Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Based on data collected in the study as described in the Results section.

claim: Among those tested at Q2 while single-vaccinated, individuals with anti-Spike levels in the lowest quintile (<18 BAU/mL) had threefold odds of post-vaccination infection compared to those in the highest quintile (≥164 BAU/mL) (OR = 2.9 [95% CI: 1.4–6.0], p=0.02), after controlling for age, sex, and number of weeks since vaccination.
source: After controlling for age, sex, and number of weeks since vaccination, those with anti-Spike levels in the lowest 80% within the sample, <164 BAU/mL, had two- to threefold odds of post-vaccination infection than those in the highest quintile, ≥164 BAU/mL, with those in the lowest quintile, <18 BAU/mL, having the largest effect size (OR = 2.9 [95% CI: 1.4–6.0], p=0.02).
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of data collected in the study.

claim: Odds of post-vaccination infection was lower in older age groups (e.g., 80+ versus 18–49, OR = 0.18 [95% CI: 0.07–0.44], p=0.002).
source: Odds of post-vaccination infection was also found to be lower in older age groups (e.g., 80+ versus 18–49, OR = 0.18 [95% CI: 0.07–0.44], p=0.002), those with serological evidence of SARS-CoV-2 infection prior to Q2 testing versus those without (OR = 0.46 [95% CI: 0.32–0.67], p=0.0009), and for those who were retired versus employed (OR = 0.49 [95% CI: 0.33–0.74], p=0.01) (full multivariable results in Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of data collected in the study.

claim: Odds of post-vaccination infection was lower in those with serological evidence of SARS-CoV-2 infection prior to Q2 testing versus those without (OR = 0.46 [95% CI: 0.32–0.67], p=0.0009).
source: Odds of post-vaccination infection was also found to be lower in older age groups (e.g., 80+ versus 18–49, OR = 0.18 [95% CI: 0.07–0.44], p=0.002), those with serological evidence of SARS-CoV-2 infection prior to Q2 testing versus those without (OR = 0.46 [95% CI: 0.32–0.67], p=0.0009), and for those who were retired versus employed (OR = 0.49 [95% CI: 0.33–0.74], p=0.01) (full multivariable results in Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of data collected in the study.

claim: Odds of post-vaccination infection was lower for those who were retired versus employed (OR = 0.49 [95% CI: 0.33–0.74], p=0.01).
source: Odds of post-vaccination infection was also found to be lower in older age groups (e.g., 80+ versus 18–49, OR = 0.18 [95% CI: 0.07–0.44], p=0.002), those with serological evidence of SARS-CoV-2 infection prior to Q2 testing versus those without (OR = 0.46 [95% CI: 0.32–0.67], p=0.0009), and for those who were retired versus employed (OR = 0.49 [95% CI: 0.33–0.74], p=0.01) (full multivariable results in Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of data collected in the study.

claim: Individuals identified as at increased risk of COVID-19 complication through the UK 'Shielded Patient List' had consistently greater odds (two- to fourfold) of having antibody levels in the lowest 10%.
source: In TwinsUK and ALSPAC, individuals identified as at increased risk of COVID-19 complication through the UK 'Shielded Patient List' had consistently greater odds (two- to fourfold) of having antibody levels in the lowest 10%.
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of data collected in the study as described in the Abstract.

claim: Individuals in both cohorts who received the AZD1222 (Oxford/AstraZeneca) vaccine versus BNT162b2 (Pfizer BioNTech) were more likely to have lower antibody levels after first vaccination (for lowest 10% in TwinsUK: (OR = 3.1, [95% CI: 1.5–6.4], p=0.02), and ALSPAC: (OR = 3.2, [95% CI: 1.4–7.7], p=0.09)).
source: Individuals in both cohorts who received the AZD1222 (Oxford/AstraZeneca) vaccine versus BNT162b2 (Pfizer BioNTech) were more likely to have lower antibody levels after first vaccination (for lowest 10% in TwinsUK: (OR = 3.1, [95% CI: 1.5–6.4], p=0.02), and ALSPAC: (OR = 3.2, [95% CI: 1.4–7.7], p=0.09)), and second vaccination (for lowest 8% in TwinsUK Q2: (OR = 3.0, [95% CI: 1.4–6.2], p=0.03), TwinsUK Q4: (OR = 45.7, [95% CI: 5.6–372], p=0.001), and ALSPAC: (OR = 20.3, [95% CI: 6.4–64.7], p=0.0001)).
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of data collected in the study.

claim: Individuals in both cohorts who received the AZD1222 (Oxford/AstraZeneca) vaccine versus BNT162b2 (Pfizer BioNTech) were more likely to have lower antibody levels after second vaccination (for lowest 8% in TwinsUK Q2: (OR = 3.0, [95% CI: 1.4–6.2], p=0.03), TwinsUK Q4: (OR = 45.7, [95% CI: 5.6–372], p=0.001), and ALSPAC: (OR = 20.3, [95% CI: 6.4–64.7], p=0.0001)).
source: Individuals in both cohorts who received the AZD1222 (Oxford/AstraZeneca) vaccine versus BNT162b2 (Pfizer BioNTech) were more likely to have lower antibody levels after first vaccination (for lowest 10% in TwinsUK: (OR = 3.1, [95% CI: 1.5–6.4], p=0.02), and ALSPAC: (OR = 3.2, [95% CI: 1.4–7.7], p=0.09)), and second vaccination (for lowest 8% in TwinsUK Q2: (OR = 3.0, [95% CI: 1.4–6.2], p=0.03), TwinsUK Q4: (OR = 45.7, [95% CI: 5.6–372], p=0.001), and ALSPAC: (OR = 20.3, [95% CI: 6.4–64.7], p=0.0001)).
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of data collected in the study.

claim: Receiving AZD1222 at second vaccination was not associated with lower antibody levels after third vaccination in TwinsUK (for lowest 10%, (OR = 1.1, [95% CI: 0.8–1.6], p=0.8)).
source: However, receiving AZD1222 at second vaccination was not associated with lower antibody levels after third vaccination in TwinsUK (for lowest 10%, (OR = 1.1, [95% CI: 0.8–1.6], p=0.8)).
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of data collected in the study.

claim: Those with longer time since vaccination at time of sampling had increased odds of lower antibody levels after second and third vaccination.
source: Those with longer time since vaccination at time of sampling had increased odds of lower antibody levels after second and third vaccination, while individuals sampled later after first vaccination had decreased odds of lower antibody levels.
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of data collected in the study.

claim: Individuals sampled later after first vaccination had decreased odds of lower antibody levels.
source: Those with longer time since vaccination at time of sampling had increased odds of lower antibody levels after second and third vaccination, while individuals sampled later after first vaccination had decreased odds of lower antibody levels.
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of data collected in the study.

claim: Lower likelihood of lower antibody levels was seen across multiple rounds of vaccination within TwinsUK for those with evidence of SARS-CoV-2 infection prior to antibody testing through serological testing (e.g., outcome: lowest 10% after third vaccination (OR = 0.45, [95% CI: 0.28–0.71], p=0.004)).
source: Lower likelihood of lower antibody levels was seen across multiple rounds of vaccination within TwinsUK for those with evidence of SARS-CoV-2 infection prior to antibody testing, either through serological testing (e.g., outcome: lowest 10% after third vaccination (OR = 0.45, [95% CI: 0.28–0.71], p=0.004)) or self-reported confirmed cases (e.g., outcome: lowest 10% after third vaccination (OR = 0.25, [95% CI: 0.13–0.45], p=0.0001)), but not for self-reported suspected cases.
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of data collected in the study.

claim: Lower likelihood of lower antibody levels was seen across multiple rounds of vaccination within TwinsUK for those with self-reported confirmed cases of SARS-CoV-2 infection (e.g., outcome: lowest 10% after third vaccination (OR = 0.25, [95% CI: 0.13–0.45], p=0.0001)).
source: Lower likelihood of lower antibody levels was seen across multiple rounds of vaccination within TwinsUK for those with evidence of SARS-CoV-2 infection prior to antibody testing, either through serological testing (e.g., outcome: lowest 10% after third vaccination (OR = 0.45, [95% CI: 0.28–0.71], p=0.004)) or self-reported confirmed cases (e.g., outcome: lowest 10% after third vaccination (OR = 0.25, [95% CI: 0.13–0.45], p=0.0001)), but not for self-reported suspected cases.
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of data collected in the study.

claim: No clear associations with lower antibody levels were seen with age, sex, or BMI in either TwinsUK or ALSPAC.
source: No clear associations with lower antibody levels were seen with age, sex, or BMI in either TwinsUK or ALSPAC.
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of data collected in the study.

claim: Within TwinsUK, pairs of identical MZ twins showed smaller average intra-pair anti-Spike antibody level differences after third vaccination versus non-identical DZ twin-pairs (median twin-pair difference = 5000 BAU/mL versus 6800 BAU/mL, p=0.0002 for MZ versus DZ).
source: Within TwinsUK, pairs of identical MZ twins showed smaller average intra-pair anti-Spike antibody level differences after third vaccination versus non-identical DZ twin-pairs (median twin-pair difference = 5000 BAU/mL versus 6800 BAU/mL, p=0.0002 for MZ versus DZ), while differences between pairs of non-related individuals were largest (median difference = 7900 BAU/mL, p<0.0001 for MZ versus non-related) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: Based on twin-pair analysis of data collected in the study and presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Differences in antibody levels between pairs of non-related individuals were largest (median difference = 7900 BAU/mL, p<0.0001 for MZ versus non-related).
source: Within TwinsUK, pairs of identical MZ twins showed smaller average intra-pair anti-Spike antibody level differences after third vaccination versus non-identical DZ twin-pairs (median twin-pair difference = 5000 BAU/mL versus 6800 BAU/mL, p=0.0002 for MZ versus DZ), while differences between pairs of non-related individuals were largest (median difference = 7900 BAU/mL, p<0.0001 for MZ versus non-related) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: Based on twin-pair analysis of data collected in the study and presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Within MZ twin-pairs discordant for 'Shielded Patient List' status, twins on the 'Shielded Patient List' had lower antibody levels after third vaccination than their co-twin (within-pair regression coefficient: –3700 BAU/mL, [95% CI: −6500, –880 BAU/mL], p=0.01).
source: Within MZ twin-pairs discordant for 'Shielded Patient List' status, twins on the 'Shielded Patient List' (within-pair regression coefficient: –3700 BAU/mL, [95% CI: −6500, –880 BAU/mL], p=0.01) had lower antibody levels after third vaccination than their co-twin (Supplementary file 9).
evidence: Based on generalised linear mixed effects regression models of twin-pair data collected in the study.

claim: Third vaccination increased absolute antibody levels for almost all individuals, and reduced relative disparities compared with earlier vaccinations.
source: Third vaccination increased absolute antibody levels for almost all individuals, and reduced relative disparities compared with earlier vaccinations.
evidence: Based on data collected in the study as described in the Abstract.

claim: Within TwinsUK, single-vaccinated individuals with the lowest 20% of anti-Spike antibody levels at initial testing had threefold greater odds of SARS-CoV-2 infection over the next 6–9 months (OR = 2.9, 95% CI: 1.4, 6.0), compared to the top 20%.
source: Within TwinsUK, single-vaccinated individuals with the lowest 20% of anti-Spike antibody levels at initial testing had threefold greater odds of SARS-CoV-2 infection over the next 6–9 months (OR = 2.9, 95% CI: 1.4, 6.0), compared to the top 20%.
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of data collected in the study as described in the Abstract.

claim: Over 75% of individuals in sub-groups associated with having the lowest antibody levels and/or higher risk of severe COVID-19 (such as shielding, frail, and/or immunosuppressed individuals) had levels above 6000 BAU/mL after third vaccination.
source: Even among sub-groups associated with having the lowest antibody levels and/or higher risk of severe COVID-19, such as shielding, frail, and/or immunosuppressed individuals, over 75% of individuals had levels above 6000 BAU/mL (Supplementary file 4), the minimum level estimated to give partial protection against omicron BA.1 variant (Dimeglio et al., 2022b).
evidence: Based on data collected in the study as described in the Discussion section.

claim: Individuals receiving AZD1222 vaccine (versus BNT162b2 [Pfizer BioNTech]) were more likely to have lower antibody levels after first and second vaccination, but this disparity was no longer evident after third vaccination.
source: Moreover, although individuals receiving AZD1222 vaccine (versus BNT162b2 [Pfizer BioNTech]) were more likely to have lower antibody levels after first and second vaccination, this disparity was no longer evident after third vaccination, consistent with lower vaccine effectiveness and increased post-vaccination infection after first or second vaccination following AZD1222 versus BNT162b2 (UKHSA, 2021; Katikireddi et al., 2022; Stouten et al., 2022), but only minor differences after third vaccination (UKHSA, 2021; Menni et al., 2022).
evidence: Based on data collected in the study and supported by citations to published research (UKHSA, 2021; Katikireddi et al., 2022; Stouten et al., 2022; Menni et al., 2022).

claim: Lower vaccine effectiveness and increased post-vaccination infection after first or second vaccination following AZD1222 versus BNT162b2 has been observed.
source: Moreover, although individuals receiving AZD1222 vaccine (versus BNT162b2 [Pfizer BioNTech]) were more likely to have lower antibody levels after first and second vaccination, this disparity was no longer evident after third vaccination, consistent with lower vaccine effectiveness and increased post-vaccination infection after first or second vaccination following AZD1222 versus BNT162b2 (UKHSA, 2021; Katikireddi et al., 2022; Stouten et al., 2022), but only minor differences after third vaccination (UKHSA, 2021; Menni et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research (UKHSA, 2021; Katikireddi et al., 2022; Stouten et al., 2022).

claim: Only minor differences in vaccine effectiveness were observed after third vaccination between AZD1222 and BNT162b2.
source: Moreover, although individuals receiving AZD1222 vaccine (versus BNT162b2 [Pfizer BioNTech]) were more likely to have lower antibody levels after first and second vaccination, this disparity was no longer evident after third vaccination, consistent with lower vaccine effectiveness and increased post-vaccination infection after first or second vaccination following AZD1222 versus BNT162b2 (UKHSA, 2021; Katikireddi et al., 2022; Stouten et al., 2022), but only minor differences after third vaccination (UKHSA, 2021; Menni et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research (UKHSA, 2021; Menni et al., 2022).

claim: Health-related variables associated with lower antibody levels were more general (self-rated poor health, immunosuppression indicators) and/or collective measures with wide-ranging criteria (e.g., 'Shielded Patient List', very frail, multimorbidity), rather than specific factors such as individual comorbidities.
source: Notably, health-related variables associated with lower antibody levels were more general (self-rated poor health, immunosuppression indicators) and/or collective measures with wide-ranging criteria (e.g., 'Shielded Patient List', very frail, multimorbidity), rather than specific factors such as individual comorbidities (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis).
evidence: Based on inference from the logistic regression analysis results described in the Discussion section.

claim: Only serology-based evidence of prior SARS-CoV-2 infection was directly associated (negatively) with subsequent post-vaccination infection between April-May 2021 and November 2021-January 2022.
source: Of the several variables associated with antibody levels, only serology-based evidence of prior SARS-CoV-2 infection was directly associated (here, negatively associated) with subsequent post-vaccination infection between April-May 2021 and November 2021-January 2022 (majority sampled before the January 2022 UK omicron variant peak).
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of data collected in the study as described in the Discussion section.

claim: No consistent associations of lower antibody levels with age or employment status were found, but a very strong age gradient (lower incidence with older age) and lower likelihood among retired (versus employed) individuals of post-vaccination infection were observed.
source: We found no consistent associations of lower antibody levels with age or employment status, but a very strong age gradient (lower incidence with older age) and lower likelihood among retired (versus employed) individuals of post-vaccination infection.
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of data collected in the study as described in the Discussion section.

claim: Risk of infection is a complex combination of SARS-CoV-2 case prevalence, individual immune response to vaccination, and individual level of exposure.
source: These results are consistent with risk of infection being a complex combination of SARS-CoV-2 case prevalence, individual immune response to vaccination, and individual level of exposure.
evidence: Based on inference from the study results described in the Discussion section.

claim: Both TwinsUK and ALSPAC (Generation 0) participants are disproportionately older, female, and more likely of white ethnicity, in comparison to the UK population.
source: Both TwinsUK and ALSPAC (Generation 0) participants are disproportionately older, female, and more likely of white ethnicity, in comparison to the UK population.
evidence: Based on known characteristics of the study cohorts as described in the Discussion section.

claim: TwinsUK (based in London) is skewed towards lower deprivation areas in south east England and ALSPAC (based in Bristol) towards south west England.
source: Geographically, TwinsUK (based in London) is skewed towards lower deprivation areas in south east England and ALSPAC (based in Bristol) towards south west England.
evidence: Based on known characteristics of the study cohorts as described in the Discussion section.

claim: The generalisability of the findings to non-white UK and international populations is limited.
source: Consequently, the generalisability of our findings to non-white UK and international populations, in addition to our ability to detect associations with smaller effect sizes, is limited.
evidence: Based on inference from the study limitations described in the Discussion section.

claim: The analyses are subject to selection biases due to use of multiple and varying data collections that rely on voluntary participation.
source: Our analyses are subject to selection biases due to use of multiple and varying data collections that rely on voluntary participation. This may cause collider bias and affect findings as outlined elsewhere (Griffith et al., 2020; Munafò et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on known methodological limitations and supported by citations to published research (Griffith et al., 2020; Munafò et al., 2018).

claim: Indicators of poorer health have been associated with lower response to COVID-19 questionnaires in ALSPAC.
source: For example, indicators of poorer health have been associated with lower response to COVID-19 questionnaires in ALSPAC (Fernández-Sanlés et al., 2021), which may bias the observed results.
evidence: Supported by citation to published research (Fernández-Sanlés et al., 2021).

claim: The replication of multiple associations with lower antibody levels across compositionally varied TwinsUK and ALSPAC cohorts and across multiple rounds of vaccination support the robustness of the findings.
source: Acknowledging the potential effects of biases, the replication of multiple associations with lower antibody levels across compositionally varied TwinsUK and ALSPAC cohorts and across multiple rounds of vaccination support the robustness of our findings.
evidence: Based on inference from the study design and results described in the Discussion section.

claim: Measurement of anti-Spike antibodies after first SARS-CoV-2 vaccination may have potential use as an early indicator to identify individuals at higher risk of a future SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: In conclusion, our results highlight the large boost across the antibody level distribution produced by third vaccination, and suggest that measurement of anti-Spike antibodies after first SARS-CoV-2 vaccination may have potential use as an early indicator to identify individuals at higher risk of a future SARS-CoV-2 infection, particularly in the many countries where vaccination roll-out is at an earlier stage.
evidence: Based on inference from the study results described in the Discussion section.

claim: Individuals who previously met UK 'Shielded Patient List' criteria had consistently lower antibody responses to vaccination than other participants.
source: Individuals who previously met UK 'Shielded Patient List' criteria had consistently lower antibody responses to vaccination than other participants, highlighting the importance of continuing to inform such individuals of their personal risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection, despite the UK government decision to end shielding guidance in April 2021 (GOV.UK, 2021).
evidence: Based on data collected in the study as described in the Discussion section.

claim: The UK government ended shielding guidance in April 2021.
source: Individuals who previously met UK 'Shielded Patient List' criteria had consistently lower antibody responses to vaccination than other participants, highlighting the importance of continuing to inform such individuals of their personal risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection, despite the UK government decision to end shielding guidance in April 2021 (GOV.UK, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to government source (GOV.UK, 2021).

claim: These findings support a policy of triple vaccination for the generation of protective antibodies.
source: These findings quantify the association between antibody level and risk of subsequent infection, and support a policy of triple vaccination for the generation of protective antibodies.
evidence: Based on inference from the study results described in the Abstract.

claim: Genetic factors influence antibody level variation after third vaccination.
source: Within TwinsUK, pairs of identical MZ twins showed smaller average intra-pair anti-Spike antibody level differences after third vaccination versus non-identical DZ twin-pairs (median twin-pair difference = 5000 BAU/mL versus 6800 BAU/mL, p=0.0002 for MZ versus DZ), while differences between pairs of non-related individuals were largest (median difference = 7900 BAU/mL, p<0.0001 for MZ versus non-related) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that MZ twins (who share 100% of their DNA) have smaller antibody level differences than DZ twins (who share ~50% of their DNA), which in turn have smaller differences than non-related individuals.

claim: Association between antibody levels and 'Shielded Patient List' status is independent of genetic and other shared factors.
source: Twin-pair regression models showed that association between antibody levels and 'Shielded Patient List' status was independent of genetic and other shared factors, after explicit adjustment for key vaccination and infection variables.
evidence: Based on generalised linear mixed effects regression models of twin-pair data collected in the study as described in the Discussion section.

claim: Individuals with evidence of SARS-CoV-2 infection prior to sampling were less likely to have lower antibody levels.
source: Individuals with evidence of SARS-CoV-2 infection prior to sampling were less likely to have lower antibody levels, consistent with previous studies that postulating that the quantity and quality of antibody response were linked to the total number of exposures to SARS-CoV-2 (Walls et al., 2022; Bates et al., 2022).
evidence: Based on data collected in the study and supported by citations to published research (Walls et al., 2022; Bates et al., 2022).

claim: The quantity and quality of antibody response are linked to the total number of exposures to SARS-CoV-2.
source: Individuals with evidence of SARS-CoV-2 infection prior to sampling were less likely to have lower antibody levels, consistent with previous studies that postulating that the quantity and quality of antibody response were linked to the total number of exposures to SARS-CoV-2 (Walls et al., 2022; Bates et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research (Walls et al., 2022; Bates et al., 2022).

claim: Median antibody levels decreased between 2 and 8 weeks after third vaccination.
source: Although median antibody levels decreased between 2 and 8 weeks after third vaccination, there was no evidence of further decline between 8 and 16 weeks (Mann-Kendall trend test in median levels at 8+ weeks, p=0.60), and high absolute levels of antibodies were sustained (8+ weeks median = 9200 BAU/mL [IQR: 5800–16000 BAU/mL], n=519).
evidence: Based on data collected in the study as described in the Results section.

claim: For individuals sampled 13–33 weeks after second vaccination, longer time since vaccination was associated with lower antibody levels.
source: Similarly, for individuals sampled 13–33 weeks after second vaccination, longer time since vaccination was also associated with lower antibody levels.
evidence: Based on data collected in the study as described in the Results section.

claim: From Q2 results, antibody levels peaked at 9 weeks after first vaccination in both TwinsUK and ALSPAC.
source: From Q2 results, antibody levels peaked at 9 weeks after first vaccination in both TwinsUK and ALSPAC.
evidence: Based on data collected in the study as described in the Results section.

claim: After second vaccination, median antibody levels breached the 250 BAU/mL assay limit from 2 weeks onwards.
source: After second vaccination, median levels breached the 250 BAU/mL assay limit from 2 weeks onwards, precluding further time assessment.
evidence: Based on data collected in the study as described in the Results section.

claim: Most double-vaccinated individuals at Q2 testing had antibody levels above the upper assay limit of 250 BAU/mL (TwinsUK: 92%, ALSPAC: 92%).
source: Most double-vaccinated individuals at Q2 testing had antibody levels above the upper assay limit of 250 BAU/mL (TwinsUK: 92%, ALSPAC: 92%).
evidence: Based on data collected in the study as described in the Methods section.

claim: One U/mL is equivalent to 1 unit of WHO standardised unit, binding antibody units per millilitre (BAU/mL).
source: One U/mL is equivalent to 1 unit of WHO standardised unit, binding antibody units per millilitre (BAU/mL) (WHO international standard: 20/136 NIBSC, 2020).
evidence: Based on established WHO standardisation and supported by citation (WHO international standard: 20/136 NIBSC, 2020).
